title: Nineteen Eighty-Four: Reflections on Totalitarianism
content:
I recently read the thought-provoking dystopian novel Nineteen Eighty-Four, and its story affected me deeply. The highly centralized society it depicts has echoes in reality: pervasive surveillance, rewritten history, and the policing of thought. Reality may not be as extreme as the novel, but similar things do exist. At a company where I once interned, there were even surveillance cameras in the toilets. I found that astonishing. 
 One line particularly struck me: those who control the past control the future, and those who control the present control the past. I was shocked by the Party's rewriting of human history. Even ancient emperors did not casually alter historians' records. These are the traces humanity leaves behind, and their truth matters. Yet a century after history is rewritten, people may accept the altered version as authentic and dismiss the real one as hearsay. How many will investigate what is true? In the end, everything may seem illusory. 
 History often appears cyclical. The Brotherhood's pamphlet describes a society in which genuine equality has never been achieved and people remain divided into upper, middle, and lower classes. Is our society so different? Each class pursues its own aims, driving the cycle onward. To me, this comes from human nature: self-interest usually dominates, shaped by our genes, and we cannot change that condition. 
 Another thought-provoking idea is that comparison allows us to recognize oppression. It reminded me of Sapiens, which describes Egyptians under Mubarak as enjoying their best material conditions yet overthrowing him after comparing their circumstances with those of Barack Obama in America. Both examples concern comparison, but show different sides of it. Comparing ourselves with others can help us recognize our worth and escape oppression; it can also intensify conflict and make life worse. 
 The Tao Te Ching also discusses comparison: refrain from elevating the worthy, valuing rare goods, or displaying objects of desire, so people do not compete, steal, or become unsettled. Perhaps happiness depends on how we manage comparison. We cannot abandon it entirely, nor compare everything. Without comparison we may lose motivation and gradually decline; constant comparison may destabilize society. Perhaps comparing ourselves with our past selves is best: becoming better tomorrow than yesterday and pursuing excellence within.

title: Sapiens: Some Current Thoughts on the World
content:
Sapiens was the first book I read outside my coursework after entering university. It profoundly challenged my view of the world and life, and remains the book that has made me think the most. Are humans truly special? How are we different from other animals? Why is society the way it is? What is money? Why do religions outlast dynasties and endure for thousands of years? What is the ‘self’? Does life have meaning, and if so, what is it? 
 In primary school, teachers told us humans were special animals because we used tools. I accepted that without much understanding. Before reading this book, I would certainly have named tool use as our greatest difference from other animals. Now I would say we have a habit of teaching and learning vast amounts of knowledge. I cannot think of a special ability unique to humans, particularly after watching films about feral children and indigenous communities. If babies born in a city and in a traditional community were exchanged, would they grow up displaying traits inconsistent with their surroundings? Probably not. I now see humans as ordinary animals whose language, abstract thought, and transmission of knowledge have developed further. 
 From the history I learned, society developed through pastoral, agricultural, and industrial stages; by modes of production, it can also be described as primitive, slave, feudal, and capitalist. Changes probably came from better tools and shifts in thought. I expect robotics and artificial intelligence to advance quickly, and technologies such as mixed reality to play a role in the future. How human ideas will change, I do not know. 
 At school I learned that money is a universal equivalent, but I had little practical understanding until reading a few personal finance books. I began to understand its reliance on a country's credit, the erosion of its value, and how bank interest is unlikely to keep up with inflation. Still, I regarded keeping money in the bank and receiving interest as risk-free. 
 As for religion, I had heard many stories from the Old and New Testaments and the Quran. I also visited a small church, where Bible stories were combined with personal experiences to demonstrate God's greatness, alongside many ideas about reincarnation. I found parts of the sermon worthwhile and others less convincing. Religion has deep insights into love and justice, but I cannot accept concepts such as reincarnation and hell. I still cannot explain why religions endure so long. 
 As I see it now, humans are ordinary animals. I believe other animals also possess things we consider uniquely ours, such as self-awareness. Does a human life have an inherent meaning? Does a monkey's? I think neither does. We are destined to disappear. Yet that idea can be despairing: if everything ends, existence seems meaningless, and much of our motivation to reproduce and strive disappears. For now, I give my life the meaning of experience—experiencing life's activities and whatever happens. 
 Thinking about the future, I see artificial intelligence as a new species humanity is creating, one that could survive longer than we do. It could inhabit different machines, communicate more efficiently, need neither oxygen nor water, and survive better in space. I believe it could be humanity's continuation.

title: Learning from Japan: Gen Z Has No Once-and-for-All Choice
content:
As someone born in 2002 who has spent time in the job market, I find the present period painful and expect the next fifteen years to be harder. Growing up, my parents said that a good university would bring a good job and an easier life. Entering work showed me otherwise: the balance of supply and demand had already changed. 
 Every year, more than ten million university graduates and over a million postgraduates enter the labor market, while the economy faces a property downturn and slower growth. We have moved from an era of expansion to one of competition over existing opportunities. People born in the 1980s and 1990s still carry large mortgages. In these circumstances, I expect the government, like Japan's, to prioritize keeping employed people in work to prevent bad bank loans and financial crisis. For Gen Z newcomers, the available jobs are likely to be outsourcing, temporary work, food delivery, and ride-hailing—unstable roles with little room to develop. 
 

 The rush toward civil service exams, public-sector jobs, and postgraduate study may not lead to safe havens, but to the next places hit by the storm. And how much do the booming AI and embodied intelligence industries really offer ordinary people like us?

title: The Road to Financial Freedom
content:
Many things matter more than money. It is simply a tool for supporting our lives, and we should not lose ourselves in its pursuit. Our time in this world is an experience: birth, aging, illness, death, love, hate, and parting. 
 After A Dog Called Money changed some of my views on money, I read another book by Bodo Schäfer, The Road to Financial Freedom. It discusses dreams, money, investing, and more. Here I am recording my  current  views on money and investing, drawing not only on this book but also on my experiences and other reading. 
 1. What is money? In everyday use, money generally means fiat currency, issued and backed by a state and recognized by law. If the state disappears, the currency may become worthless paper. To me, a larger and more stable state tends to have a more stable currency. Yet governments can issue more money, reducing its purchasing power through inflation. That is why I value globally recognized forms of money above a single country's currency: gold and silver, recognized for thousands of years, seem more valuable to me than the currency of a country with only decades of history. 
 2. My current investing principles 
 Always keep at least CNY 20,000 in cash as a financial cushion 
 
 Invest in gold and the S&P 500 mainly through long-term holdings and regular contributions 
 
 For Chinese A-shares, first choose an industry, then its leading companies; buy in batches near historical lows and sell when the expected return is reached 
 
 
 3. My dreams 
 A healthy, strong body 
 
 Financial independence and freedom 
 
 A stable family life 
 
 Work in robotics, connecting the physical and digital worlds 
 
 Read many books

title: Guns, Germs, and Steel: Exploring the Ultimate Causes of Human Societies
content:
I. Introduction After finishing Sapiens, I saw a comment in Douban's reviews saying  ‘This book does not deserve such a high rating; Guns, Germs, and Steel is better.’  That put the book on my reading list, where it waited until I finally finished it a few days ago. The book asks why Europe conquered the world. It starts with crops and animal domestication, moves through language, writing, and the characteristics of inventions that get adopted, and surveys societies in China, Japan, Korea, Pacific islands, and different parts of Africa. 
 II. A deeper exploration 1. How fewer than 200 Spaniards conquered an Inca Empire with an army of 80,000 In 1532, Francisco Pizarro led fewer than 200 soldiers to capture the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca, despite the emperor's tens of thousands of troops. Atahualpa filled a room with gold to buy his freedom, but Pizarro broke his promise and executed him. The emperor's death left the Inca Empire without a leader, rapidly undermining central authority. The Spaniards advanced south and eventually occupied the capital, Cusco. 
 Pizarro's victory can be attributed to steel, horses, and culture. Before Europeans invaded the Americas, the Inca had never seen horses. Mounted charges had an enormous psychological impact. Spanish steel swords could pierce Inca hide armor, while Inca bronze and stone weapons could not penetrate Spanish armor. The Inca had not seen white people before; some even regarded them as divine messengers and did not understand their colonial aims. 
 Germs were another major cause of the empire's collapse. Smallpox and other diseases arrived with Europeans. They killed far more people than the conquest's direct warfare and violence, greatly weakening the empire. 
 Looking for ultimate causes 

 Why did the diseases brought by Spaniards kill so many Indigenous Americans? Europeans kept livestock, and prolonged contact with animals had given them immunity to diseases. Why did Europe have livestock when the Americas did not? Its agriculture produced enough crops to support animal husbandry. 
 Why did Spaniards acquire steelmaking and horse domestication first? European agriculture could support people who specialized in steelmaking and horse breeding. But why was agriculture more developed in Europe than in the Americas? Europe's geography suited crop growth. Eurasia's east–west axis involves relatively little change in latitude, helping crops spread. 
 2. Why humans shifted from hunting and gathering to food production The book does not give a definitive answer, but suggests five main factors: declining access to wild foods; increasing access to domesticable wild plants, making cultivation more rewarding; the long-term development of technologies that made food production more beneficial; the relationship between rising population density and food production; and, finally, the replacement of hunter-gatherer groups by farmers. 
 3. Why some animals can be domesticated and others cannot: the Anna Karenina principle Just as  ‘happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way’,  domesticable animals meet the necessary conditions, while undomesticable animals each fail in their own way. Domestication depends on many factors: diet, growth rate, mating behavior, temperament, tendency to panic, and aspects of social organization. Most domesticated animals originated in Eurasia. 
 

 4. How new technology gets adopted 
 Greater economic benefit than existing technology 
 
 Social value and prestige 
 
 Compatibility with vested interests 
 
 How easily its advantages can be seen 
 5. Language and writing As vehicles for communication and knowledge, I consider language and writing humanity's most important inventions. Writing lets us access information and knowledge from hundreds or thousands of years ago. Civilization develops through that accumulated knowledge, while language is our most important bridge for communication. 
 6. Why China did not conquer the world China invented gunpowder and the compass, and once led the world in shipbuilding, as Zheng He's voyages show. Why, then, did it not conquer the world? China at the time saw itself as vast, resource-rich, and self-sufficient. Maritime ventures offered low returns relative to their cost and faced piracy and anti-Qing forces in Taiwan. With no clear benefit, China gradually restricted seafaring and closed itself off. Europe, by contrast, consisted of competing small states that sought expansion abroad. 
 III. Closing thoughts Drawing on experiences in New Guinea and neighboring islands, together with historical and archaeological evidence, the author develops a tightly argued explanation: the ultimate cause of human societies' present differences lies in the environment, or continental axes. It also left me wondering: under complete causal determinism, is the world's course fixed? Is everything that happens to us already written into the universe's script? If so, why does the microscopic world contain seemingly random phenomena such as the uncertainty principle and delayed-choice experiments?

title: A Little Dog Changed How I Think About Money
content:
To borrow a popular saying, this fairy tale about money may seem ‘a little childish for primary school children, but just right for university students’. It follows a dog named Money and a girl named Kira, showing how Money teaches her to manage her finances. Reading it, I felt I was learning alongside Kira. 
 Here are some of the book's rules about money, as I understand them: 
 
 Dream savings jars 
 
 Write down your wishes and choose the three you most want to fulfill 
 
 Imagine the moment your wish comes true 
 
 Prepare a savings jar for each dream and believe you can achieve it 
 
 Start right now 
 
 
 
 Keep a success journal 
 
 If you do not believe you can do something, you will not try—so believe in yourself 
 
 Recall what you have already achieved 
 
 Record your achievements regularly;  the original says to write five entries every day, but I think recording them regularly and freely is enough 
 
 
 
 Perseverance 
 
 Anyone can make money when things go well; adversity is the real test. —From the book 
 
 Keep doing these things even when life is going well, regularly at a fixed time each day 
 
 When you decide to do something, start within 72 hours if possible 
 
 Never borrow for consumption 
 
 Earn money doing what you enjoy 
 
 
 
 Never kill your goose (the principal that earns interest) 
 
 Save part of your income to build your own goose 
 
 Put another portion into your dream savings jars 
 
 Never kill your goose 
 
 Stocks, funds, and gold can also be geese—better geese 
 
 Investment returns only become real when you sell 
 
 
 
 Seven principles for good character 
 
 Be friendly and approachable 
 
 Take responsibility 
 
 Treat others kindly 
 
 Help and give 
 
 Be grateful 
 
 Keep learning 
 
 Be trustworthy 
 
 
 
 
 I read A Dog Called Money a long time ago. It introduced me to economic thinking, and I began saving, keeping accounts, and investing. Later I read other books on money, whose ideas echoed this one. I became curious about its author, Bodo Schäfer, and read his more advanced book The Road to Financial Freedom. I plan to write about it later. 
 Writing these notes prompted me to revisit the book. Looking back, it has helped me a lot. My investment earnings have been modest, but the experience is remarkable. I hope one day to live on investment income and achieve financial freedom.

title: The Origin of ‘Keeping Dreams’
content:
In junior high school, I read an unforgettable novel. I have forgotten its title, but the story remains vivid. In the protagonist's hometown, people stopped dreaming after a certain age. Guided by his last dream, his father left on a journey to find those lost dreams while the protagonist was still a child. When he grew up, he set out on the same quest. 
 On this extraordinary journey, he went through many adventures. He was tricked into working in a coal mine and encountered mysterious creatures such as unicorns. Eventually he returned home, but kept searching for the lost dreams and was finally reunited with his father. My memory of the ending, however, has become hazy. 
 As the years passed, the book's influence on me grew. The phrase ‘Keeping Dreams, Weathered by Wind’ gradually took on a special meaning. I split it into ‘Keeping Dreams’ and ‘Weathered by Wind’, giving each its own significance. By coincidence, ‘LM’, the initials of ‘Liu Meng’, looks rather like my initials ‘WJJ’ turned upside down. I decided to use LM as my online alias and designed a distinctive logo for myself. 
 This alias and logo represent that unforgettable reading experience and have become part of my growing up. Whenever I see them, I remember the captivating novel and its adventurous search for dreams.

title: Me and Ms. Luo
content:
I met Ms. Luo a month ago while lying in the courtyard, sunbathing, snacking, and contemplating the future—in other words, daydreaming. A soft, clear voice interrupted my wandering thoughts. Before me stood a figure rather unlike her voice: a sturdy Siamese cat. Such a beautiful cat is rare in the countryside. I broke off some steamed bread and offered it to her, but she apparently considered it beneath her. She ignored it, circled me a few times, and left. 
 After that, I often spent afternoons sunbathing in the courtyard and sometimes met Ms. Luo on her strolls. I always heard her clear voice before seeing her. She would come over and rub against me, ignoring the food I offered. She played nearby, nuzzled me, purred contentedly, and eventually wandered off.

title: Why Dynasties Last Three Centuries but Families Endure a Millennium
content:
Introduction I happened to learn that Qian Xuesen, the ‘father of Chinese aerospace’; Qian Weichang, a founder of modern Chinese mechanics; Qian Sanqiang, a leading figure in China's atomic bomb program; chemistry Nobel laureate Roger Tsien; and Confucian scholar Qian Mu all came from the same family. Qian Xuesen and Roger Tsien were relatives across generations, while Qian Weichang was Qian Mu's nephew. After imperial collapse and cultural purges, in an era when most Chinese families started from farming, such a family's achievements astonished me. 
 I explored the family's origins, development, and teachings, then turned to Records of the Grand Historian to look for other notable families. I found that the five ancient emperors—the Yellow Emperor, Zhuanxu, Ku, Yao, and Shun—were related, and that the Xia, Shang, and Zhou rulers all descended from the Yellow Emperor. Thirty of the work's 130 chapters concern hereditary houses, nearly a quarter of the book. This reveals a family influence in Chinese civilization that school history alone had not shown me. 
 The Qian family: seek no benefit for yourself alone; seek what benefits all After the Tang collapsed, regional military rulers divided the land, ushering in the turmoil of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms. Qian Liu began as an illicit salt trader before joining the military. Through military ability, he gained control of armed forces and thirteen prefectures in the two Zhejiang regions, receiving the title King of Wuyue from Later Liang. He adopted a policy of protecting the territory and its people while maintaining good relations with the central powers. His successors later surrendered the territory to the Song, sparing the region further warfare. 
 The Qian family has continued from Qian Liu to the present, for more than a millennium. Why can it endure so long when Chinese dynasties struggle to last three hundred years? With my limited understanding, perhaps struggles for imperial power were fiercer, while the Qian family's teachings and traditions supported its continuity. Appendix:  The Qian Family Teachings 
 After this brief exploration, I wondered whether this could be the only such family in Chinese history. I remembered the hereditary houses in Records of the Grand Historian, but did not expect to encounter what seemed the largest family of all as soon as I opened it: the Yellow Emperor's family. 
 Records of the Grand Historian: the Five Emperors and the Xia, Yin, and Zhou annals I had assumed the ancient Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors led different tribes. The Five Emperors annals instead presented them as one family. Even the supposed abdication system looked like power passing within that family. As Shennong's line under the Yan Emperor weakened, the Yellow Emperor Xuanyuan defeated Chiyou, gained the ‘Mandate of Heaven’, and began the line of rule extending to the Zhou. 
 
 The power of families Mentioning great families used to make me think first of Britain or northern Europe. Yet China has nurtured countless families too. Their power is less visible in modern life, but it has never disappeared.

title: What I Live For
content:
Long ago I began asking myself: if the universe will end in heat death, humanity will disappear, and my traces will probably vanish within a century of my death, what am I living for? What is my purpose? My answer is experience. I treat everything that happens to me as an experience, a feeling that will fade with time. To enrich those experiences, I wrote a personal life list. Fewer than ten items seemed enough; with too many, some would probably remain undone. Unfulfilled wishes would bring the suffering of wanting what one cannot have, as Buddhism describes it. 
 My life list 
 
 First, become financially independent, with my own income and savings, so I can support myself without relying on my parents or family. Only with financial independence do I feel truly independent and whole as a person. After working for a year following graduation, I had saved enough to live for a while without a job. That is my present situation. 
 
 Maintain good habits so my body stays healthy and my mind clear while I work through this list. 
 
 Experience love. I have experienced it and left it with dignity. 
 
 Experience different ways of living. After leaving my job, I spent a month living in Weihai. I also considered staying in Kunming, Yunnan, for a while. I will see how things go: if time and money allow, I will stay; otherwise, a trip will do. 
 
 See different parts of the world. Growing up on the plains, I longed for mountains. Now I have climbed many mountains and seen the sea, and I have few regrets. Other landscapes can come as opportunities arise. 
 
 Read many good books. Books cross time and space, carrying their authors' thoughts and spirit. Once written, a book no longer belongs solely to its author: it becomes a conversation with the reader. I enjoy this exchange. Communicating with minds that once existed, or are still briefly here, makes me feel that life and spirit can extend beyond their limits. 
 
 
 
 Books I have read: 
 
 Those that deeply influenced me: Yuval Noah Harari: Sapiens, Homo Deus, 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, and Nexus; George Orwell: Nineteen Eighty-Four and Animal Farm; The Social Animal; Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!; The Feynman Lectures on Physics 
 
 Books on economics and finance Bodo Schäfer: A Dog Called Money and The Road to Financial Freedom; Principles; The Money Wand: Modern Jewish Business Methods; A Guide to Investing in Index Funds 
 
 Books on living: Designing Your Life; Second Growth; Don't Overthink It; The Willpower Instinct; Sleep; Why We Sleep; 
 
 Literature I enjoy Fish Have No Feet; Submarines in the Night; Selected Misty Poems; Summer, Fireworks, and My Corpse; Dai Jianye Reads Laozi; The Seventh Day; To Live; Gu Cheng's Poems; Haizi's Poems; Home Is Where the Heart Is at Peace; A Maverick Pig; and others 
 
 
 
 Currently reading: The Feynman Lectures on Physics; Not Blown Down by the Wind 
 
 Books I only partly understand: Thus Spoke Zarathustra; the Old Testament; the New Testament; the Quran Some books are a pleasure for their beautiful language. Others prompt thoughts about the world and leave a lasting influence. Still others teach knowledge and principles that help me live better. I do not think I will put books aside for the rest of my limited life. 
 
 
 
 Raise a child. I once thought about life's pressures, mutual suspicion, conflicting desires, and family disputes. Finding a supportive and trusting partner seemed difficult. Childbirth would cause a partner pain, and raising a child takes time, money, and energy; life without children might be easier. Later, though, I came to feel that nurturing a life and watching a child grow could be wonderful. It would require my partner's agreement and some financial stability, so I will let circumstances decide. It is not essential. 
 
 Meet death. Looking back on my twenty-four years, I feel my life has been reasonably rich. Even if I died in the next moment, I would have few regrets. I only hope not to suffer too much beforehand. 
 
 
 Looking over my life list, I have completed more than half and feel fewer attachments. For the rest of my life, I will eat, sleep, read, and work well, and let things take their course. 
 Without my education, I might want to repair small objects such as watches and phones. A few centuries earlier, perhaps I would have been a carpenter. But living in this era, I think spending my remaining time studying robotics would be interesting.

title: Tian Miaomiao
content:
Tian Miaomiao was born in a remote village in northern Henan, the fourth child after two sisters and a brother, with perhaps more younger siblings to follow. A month or two after her birth, the family had no food to spare. Her parents handed her over to a local wealthy household for a tael of silver, to be a companion to their child. 
 The household's son, Liu Meng, adored his companion. He played with her every day and shared his food and toys. Despite his parents' strong objections, he even took her into the family's ancestral shrine. 
 Later, Liu Meng went abroad to study, and his contact with Miaomiao gradually dwindled. Seeing this, his parents wanted to drive her out but feared upsetting him. Instead, they treated her more harshly, often withholding food and occasionally beating and scolding her. Still remembering the Liu Meng of her childhood, Miaomiao refused to leave. 
 As Miaomiao approached twenty, the household arranged to marry her off. Aware of her position, she agreed. Years later Liu Meng returned. By then Miaomiao had three children, though she still worked as a servant in the household. On learning this, Liu Meng felt both surprised and that it somehow made sense. 
 The first people Liu Meng saw on returning were Miaomiao's three children, rather than Miaomiao herself. Her husband had abandoned her before their third child was born. While working at the household, she had to bring the children along and let them play nearby. 
 Liu Meng immediately knew whose children they were: they looked so much like the little Miaomiao he remembered. A few minutes later, Miaomiao came in. Seeing him, she froze for a long while, said nothing, and quietly followed him as though she were merely another servant. When she tried to follow him into the ancestral shrine, he stopped her outside. At that moment, Tian Miaomiao knew they were no longer who they had once been. 
 The next day, Tian Miaomiao left her position. Where she went with her three children, I do not know. 
 P.S. Miao'er is my cat. Since I refused to let her into my room, I have not seen her or her kittens again. I hope she is happy out there.

title: Learning About and Trying Cryptocurrency
content:
Learning about BTC On October 11, 2025, after  Trump announced an additional 100% tariff on China , the cryptocurrency market experienced cascading liquidations, and BTC fell from over USD 120,000 to over USD 80,000. Hearing this, I looked into BTC with the idea of buying the dip and joined Binance to try some small trades. 
 Understanding the technology I first studied  the Bitcoin white paper read it once, XD . BTC builds its framework from a timestamp server, proof of work (PoW), and a blockchain network. Participating in bookkeeping and PoW can generate new BTC. The mining reward halves every 210,000 blocks, limiting the total supply to 21 million coins and preventing dilution through unlimited issuance. The original design used  Merkle tree  pruning to reclaim disk space so modest computers could participate. The present network, however, relies on full nodes rather than fully following that vision. Competition for PoW computing power has driven up costs and produced specialized mining hardware, leaving ordinary people largely unable to take part in the core process. With one block every ten minutes, transaction speed also falls short of real-world needs. Secondary networks may eventually address this. 
 Historical background Why propose such a system? The 2008 financial crisis brought bank failures, followed by quantitative easing and currency depreciation. Perhaps the developer was affected by that disaster. I see the proposal as a response to collapsing trust in banks: when states print money and reduce people's purchasing power, a decentralized currency with a fixed supply aims to prevent that erosion. 
 Summary Overall, BTC's fixed supply of 21 million, first-mover advantage, and growing global consensus underpin its role as a store of value. Yet ten-minute blocks, congestion, wasted computing power through PoW competition, and the challenge it poses to governments make me doubt its use as everyday currency. Technologies such as the Lightning Network may address some weaknesses. The more I learn about BTC, the less reliable the system seems to me. We will see what the future brings. 
 Trying Binance Crypto: exchanges that are easy to enter Before entering crypto, I had traded funds and Chinese A-shares for more than a year. Unlike the CNY 500,000 threshold for access to Hong Kong stocks and the various restrictions on US stocks, crypto exchanges run around the clock, allow unrestricted trading, make shorting easy, and encourage futures trading. This was my first experience with futures. 
 Futures: a wild gambling game Futures let a small amount of capital take on leverage of tens or even hundreds of times, magnifying both gains and losses. When losses approach the initial margin, positions are forcibly closed, or ‘liquidated’. Cross-margin modes can use all futures funds or even all assets as collateral to avoid liquidation when losses exceed the initial margin. In extreme conditions, however, cascading liquidations can wipe out everything. Event contracts are an even purer gamble: choose ten minutes, thirty minutes, an hour, or a day and bet on a cryptocurrency's direction. A winning bet pays 80% or 85% of the stake; a losing bet wipes it out. 
 Common crypto scams 1. Honeypot tokens can be bought but not sold. Newcomers are often lured by apparent high returns, only to find they cannot withdraw anything. 2. Scammers impersonate support staff or build a friendly rapport, promise to activate a service or help you earn money, then send fake links. 3. Someone posts a screenshot claiming to be quitting crypto and giving away the remaining balance. After logging in, you are told to deposit a withdrawal fee first. Even after paying, you cannot withdraw, and the fee is stolen. 
 Greed is often what makes people vulnerable to scams

title: Haizi's Poems That I Cannot Understand
content:
Excerpts In which shoe will I wake tomorrow? 
 I cannot give up happiness Or, instead, I live on suffering Half Buried 
 1985 
 
 
 September 
 Wildflowers cover the grassland that witnessed the gods' death The wind far away is farther than the faraway My instrument sobs; there are no tears I return this distant distance to the grassland One is called wood, the other horsetail My instrument sobs; there are no tears 
 Only in death does the distance gather into wildflowers The bright moon, a mirror above the grassland, reflects a thousand years My instrument sobs; there are no tears Alone, riding across the grassland 
 1986 
 
 
 Village 
 Village—in a village rich with grain, I settle down The fewer things within my reach, the better! Cherish the village at dusk, cherish the village in rain A cloudless sky, like my eternal sorrow 
 1986 
 
 
 A Poem Dedicated to the Night 
 You come from afar; I am going far away The distant journey passes through here There is nothing in the sky Why does it comfort me? 
 The desolate earth after the harvest People have taken away a year's harvest Taken the grain and ridden away on the horses Those left in the fields are buried deep 
 1989.2.2 
 
 Personal Reflections I first knew Haizi through Facing the Sea, with Spring Blossoms and Taking Dreams as Horses. His cheerful smile on the cover of Haizi's Poems once made me imagine him as an outgoing person, longing for freedom like a seagull. 
 I used to think ‘Haizi’ symbolized a seabird, perhaps a gull. But when I learned his real name, Zha Haisheng—‘born of the sea’—I thought that might be the real origin of his pen name. 
 He entered Peking University at fifteen and died by suicide on the railway at twenty-five. 
 He wrote of a cloudless sky resembling his eternal sorrow, and of an empty sky that nonetheless offered comfort. 
 I cannot understand Haizi's poems, nor do I want to understand them fully. I simply experience their poetry.
